articles.title: Decoding Spikes From Multiunit Data
articles.content: Communication and control in biological systems is mediated by the timing of discharges –spikes– from excitable cells such as neurons and muscle fibers. Each spike is associated to a characteristic waveform that can be captured by sensors. The waveform's characteristics depend on the cell's biophysical properties and the recording modality. Depending on the technique, e.g., electrical recordings with electrodes, optical imaging, ultrasound, the observed signals are mixtures of waveforms emitted from active cells/sources (multiunit data/signals). Recovering the timing and identity of these sources (multiunit or spike decoding) is central to neuroscience, clinical diagnostics, and neural interfacing, yet it remains challenging due to waveform superposition, non-stationarity, limited training labels, and the computational demands of high-density recordings. This review provides a unified methodological perspective on spike decoding by formalizing the problem as a sparse source separation task under a convolutive mixing model. Rather than organizing the literature by application domain, we group and critically compare methods by their underlying principles: classical spike sorting, Bayesian and probabilistic inference, blind source separation, and data-driven approaches, including deep learning and hybrid schemes. For each class of methods, we present the core mathematical formulation and algorithmic strategies and discuss assumptions and limitations. Our synthesis highlights parallels in signal processing across physical recording modalities and clarifies when and why particular approaches succeed or fail. By bridging previously compartmentalized literature, this survey aims to accelerate crosspollination of ideas between application areas and to provide a roadmap for selecting, adapting, and advancing decoding methods across diverse multiunit recording modalities.

articles.title: Separation, isolation, and membrane lipid profiling of selectively vulnerable and resilient neurons
articles.content: Certain neurons are more susceptible to pathogenic stressors and degenerate, while others remain resilient in neurodegenerative diseases. However, the mechanisms underlying this cell-to-cell heterogeneity in neuronal vulnerability remain unclear, primarily due to challenges in isolating vulnerable and resilient neurons to characterize their properties. In this study, we report the development of a novel cell-labeling method utilizing two cell-impermeable dyes to identify vulnerable and resilient neurons in culture, which are subsequently separated and isolated via fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). As a proof-of-concept of a mechanistic study, we conducted lipidomic analysis to determine whether the lipid composition of membranes differs between vulnerable and resilient neurons to oxidative stress. This simple but unique method sets the groundwork for investigating the molecular underpinnings of selective neuronal vulnerability, which could inform new diagnostic strategies and therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases.
articles.author: Sadek, M., Yokomizo, M., Williams, E., Wieckiewicz, N., Owusu Kwarteng, D., Das, S., Bennett, R. E., Gomez-Isla, T., Maesako, M.

articles.title: Dual Roles of Interferon-γ Receptor in Somatostatin Interneurons at Baseline and During Inflammation
articles.content: Background: Neuropsychiatric disorders such as major depressive disorder show converging evidence of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) dysfunction, including consistent reductions in somatostatin (SST) interneuron markers. SST interneurons are selectively vulnerable to inflammation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}), a pro-inflammatory cytokine implicated in mood and anxiety disorders, signals through the IFN-{gamma} receptor (IFNGR), which is expressed in neurons. We tested whether IFNGR signaling in SST interneurons regulates anxiety-like and cognitive behavior and prevents inflammation-induced molecular deficits. Methods: We generated mice with conditional deletion of IFNGR from SST cells and assessed anxiety-like behavior using elevated plus maze and working memory using Y-maze at baseline and after lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced inflammation. Expression of SST-related, neurotrophic, synaptic, and glial markers was quantified. Results: At baseline and after LPS-induced inflammation, IFNGR deletion in SST cells increased anxiety-like behavior without affecting working memory. In control mice, LPS reduced Sst (p=0.0006), neuropeptide Y (Npy) (p=0.0022), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) (p<0.0001), and synapsin 1 (Syn1) (p=0.0150); these reductions were not significant in mice lacking IFNGR in SST cells. Knockouts also showed lower baseline Bdnf, Syn1, Gephyrin (Gphn), and allograft inflammatory factor 1 (Aif1, encoding Iba1) than controls. Conclusions: IFNGR signaling in SST cells plays a dual role: supporting normal behavior and molecular homeostasis while mediating LPS-induced molecular deficits. These findings link immune signaling to the GABAergic dysfunction implicated in major depressive disorder and suggest IFNGR signaling in SST cells may regulate cortical microcircuit integrity at baseline and during inflammatory challenge.
articles.author: Rezaei, S., Tomoda, T., Marcotte, M., Prevot, T. D., Banasr, M., Bansal, Y., Ezzeddine, A., Guan, A., Vieira, E., Sibille, E.

articles.title: Dizocilpine-derived K2060 exhibits enhanced blockage at NMDA receptors with impaired Mg2+ block and provides strong protection against audiogenic seizures
articles.content: Background and Purpose: Voltage-dependent Mg2+ block is a defining feature of the GluN1/GluN2 subtype of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs). We tested how impaired Mg2+ block at GluN1/GluN2A receptors mutated at the GluN2A-N615 position modifies inhibition by dizocilpine-derived K2060 compared with clinically used memantine and ketamine. Experimental Approach: Electrophysiological recordings were performed on recombinant wild-type (WT) and mutated GluN1/GluN2A receptors expressed in HEK293T cells. Acute hippocampal slice electrophysiology and behavioural studies were conducted in WT and knock-in GluN2A-N615S mice. In vivo tolerability and efficacy were evaluated using open field testing, prepulse inhibition (PPI), and protection against audiogenic seizures (AGS). Key Results: Mg2+ reduced the apparent potency of all three blockers and slowed onset at the GluN1/GluN2A-WT receptor. These Mg2+-dependent effects were absent or markedly reduced at the GluN1/GluN2A-N615S and GluN1/GluN2A-N615K receptors. In addition, K2060 showed slower unbinding and greater trapping than memantine. In hippocampal slices from GluN2A-N615S mice, K2060 exhibited enhanced but slower onset inhibition than memantine and ketamine. In vivo, K2060 caused no overt behavioural disruption at 5 mg/kg (i.p.) and did not further disrupt PPI. All three blockers protected GluN2A-N615S mice against AGS at 5 mg/kg (i.p.); only K2060 remained protective at 1 mg/kg (i.p.). Conclusions and Implications: Impaired Mg2+; block removes a physiological constraint on the action of NMDAR blockers. K2060 exhibited the most favourable pharmacological profile, supporting its further evaluation for studies with NMDAR hyperfunction models. Additional pharmacokinetic, safety, and disease-model studies are warranted.

articles.title: Exploratory Proteomics of Brain Extracellular Vesicle Enriched Preparations After LPS Challenge and miRNA Associated Vesicle Administration
articles.content: We used brain extracellular vesicle (EV) proteomics to identify protein responses to acute neuroinflammation and an EV-based microRNA intervention. Rats received vehicle, intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS), or LPS followed by an intravenous EV formulation containing anti-inflammatory microRNAs (miRNAs). Brains were collected 24 h after LPS or vehicle administration, and three independently processed animal-derived EV-enriched preparations per group were analyzed by label-free proteomics. Across all nine samples, 953 protein groups had complete normalized abundance measurements. Compared with vehicle controls, LPS exposure was associated with 227 exploratory protein changes, comprising 95 increases and 132 decreases at nominal P < 0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change >= log2(1.5). Increased proteins were enriched for translation-related annotations, whereas decreased proteins were enriched for plasma-membrane annotations. These LPS-associated changes did not remain significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction at a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of q < 0.05. Following treatment, 119 of the 227 candidates were closer to control abundance on the log2 scale; 23 candidates also showed nominal treatment-versus-LPS differences. Lamb2 and Ptgfrn were the two proteins that differed significantly between treated and LPS-only animals after FDR correction, identifying them as priorities for further validation. Nevertheless, 174 proteins differed significantly between treated animals and vehicle controls, and analysis across the measured proteins did not demonstrate an overall shift toward control values. Thus, the intervention was associated with specific protein responses, but treated animals retained substantial differences from controls. This study identifies candidate markers for investigating treatment responses in brain EV-enriched preparations and demonstrates the value of examining individual proteins alongside broader proteomic changes. Independent validation is needed to determine their functional relevance and distinguish miRNA-specific effects from contributions of the administered EV carrier.
articles.author: Brown, K., Wang, Y., Shan, Z., Bi, L.

articles.title: Intrastriatal injection of amplified Lewy body dementia (LBD) fibrils in mice results in accumulation of fibrils with LBD structure and neurodegeneration
articles.content: The defining neuropathologic feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) is alpha-synuclein (Asyn) fibril accumulation in Lewy bodies (LBs) and Lewy neurites (LNs). Recently, we developed a method to amplify Asyn fibrils derived from human post-mortem LBD brain tissue and determined that the structure of amplified Asyn fibrils is highly similar to the structure of fibrils directly isolated from LBD brain tissue. We examined whether injection of these fibrils into humanized Asyn mice recapitulates pathologic Asyn fibril accumulation with human LBD Asyn fibril structure. We utilized mice containing a null allele in the mouse Snca gene and a human SNCA transgene. Intrastriatal injection of amplified Asyn fibrils derived from 3 different LBD autopsy cases resulted in cytoplasmic and neuritic phospho-Asyn accumulation in the striatum, cortex, and amygdala bilaterally at 3mpi. Fibril injections produced a reduction in the number of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, with LB-like inclusions in surviving neurons, and produced impaired sensorimotor function as measured on the accelerating rotarod test. Fibril accumulation increased 3.6-fold between 1 and 3 months post-injection (mpi) and was relatively stable between 3 and 5 mpi. We amplified fibrils from mouse brain tissue 5 mpi and collected single-particle cryo-EM data. High resolution 3D structural information could not be obtained because of the lack of helical twist, but comparison of the cryo-EM 2D class averages with those derived from amplified fibrils prepared from human LBD tissue revealed multiple matching classes, indicating that the Lewy fold is maintained in the fibrils that accumulate in mouse brain tissue. Our findings demonstrate an approach to model the accumulation of Asyn fibrils with LBD structure in mice, providing a platform for investigating disease mechanisms, imaging biomarkers, and therapeutics targeting Asyn in PD/LBD.
articles.author: Bagade, A. V., Miller, R., Dearborn, J. T., Basore, K., Summers, B., Readnour, B., Koelling, M., O'Shea, J., Wright, E. R., Dhavale, D. D., Kotzbauer, P. T.

articles.title: Postprandial hypertriglyceridemia activates microglia to promote satiety via an ASC dependent signaling.
articles.content: Reactive microglia are commonly considered neurotoxic and detrimental for brain functioning. Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet strongly activates microglia, disrupts the central control of energy metabolism, contributes to obesity, and promotes cognitive decline. In this study we report an unexpected beneficial function of microglia reaction at the time scale of a meal, whereby they promote satiety in a macronutrient-dependent manner. We show that murine microglia react to ingested dietary fat within three hours. Specifically, postprandial hypertriglyceridemia induced microglial hyper-ramification alongside with a transcriptional reprogramming promoting communication with neurons. This effect occurs in discrete brain areas, including the hypothalamus and the brainstem, which control hunger. Remarkably, microglia-specific genetic ablation of Apoptosis-associated Speck-like protein containing a CARD (named ASC), a master regulator of metabolism, immune function and cell shape, profoundly alters satiety following high-fat food consumption. These results reveal that microglia engage an immune signaling pathway to rapidly alert the neural circuits and activate an anorectic response that limits overconsumption of dietary fat. Unexpectedly, this regulatory process is sexually dimorphic, present in males only. Furthermore, we found that the postprandial microglial reaction is bypassed during obesity, providing a new therapeutic target to treat maladaptive eating disorders.

articles.title: Integration of Neuroimaging and Histopathology in a Squirrel Monkey Model of Spontaneous Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy and Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities
articles.content: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a prevalent cerebrovascular pathology in AD and contributes to amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), a major complication of current anti-amyloid immunotherapy. Despite its growing clinical importance, critical gaps remain in the development of reliable biomarkers for antemortem diagnosis of CAA. Squirrel monkeys (SQMs) are a valuable non-human primate model with translational relevance due to their universal propensity to develop abundant CAA and spontaneous ARIA in geriatric animals. The present study employed R2*, the apparent transverse relaxation rate, which is sensitive to susceptibility-related tissue properties, including iron content and blood oxygenation levels, to monitor age-related brain pathology in SQMs with varying CAA severity. Young, early geriatric, and late geriatric SQMs underwent 7T MRI using a dual-purpose T2*-w 3D multi-gradient-echo sequence for high-resolution anatomy and quantitative R2* mapping, alongside T2-w/FLAIR imaging. Whole-brain and gray matter R2* increased with age. In contrast, white matter R2* showed an initial increase followed by a late-life reversal, likely reflecting age-related changes in myelin integrity, tissue microstructure, and tissue water content. MRI-histopathology correlation linked T2*-w MRI hypointensities to CAA-positive iron-laden vessels associated with perivascular inflammation and, in some cases, hemosiderin deposits. Here we confirmed the occurrence of ARIA-H and ARIA-E events in geriatric animals. SQMs provided a valuable opportunity to examine the underlying pathology of spontaneous ARIA-E, revealing distinctive tissue signatures associated with its manifestation. ARIA-E hyperintensities were characterized by reactive gliosis and BBB disruption, whereas more advanced lesions exhibited perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and evidence of myelin and axonal injury. The current study presents compelling evidence linking R2* alterations with CAA severity and ARIA-related tissue injury, providing a foundation for further advancing early detection of CAA, ARIA risk assessment, and treatment strategies.
articles.author: Wadghiri, Y. Z., Khan, S., Soliman, M. T., Szabo, J., Murray, A., Patel, A. G., Kingsley, C., Swain, J., Nehete, P. N., Veraart, J., Mulholland, M. M., Hopkins, W. D., Wisniewski, T., Scholtzova, H.

articles.title: Adaptive co-transmission shapes sensory encoding and behavior
articles.content: Co-transmission expands the chemical repertoire of neurons, but whether coexisting neurotransmitters can be independently organized and remodeled by experience to control distinct aspects of behavior remains unclear. Here, we address this question in the AFD thermosensory neuron of Caenorhabditis elegans, which directs navigation toward a learned temperature preference. We find that glutamatergic and cholinergic vesicular transporters coexist within individual presynaptic boutons but differ in axonal trafficking, subsynaptic organization, and dependence on presynaptic machinery. Sensory experience differentially regulates the two systems: animals trained to prefer higher temperatures exhibit increased VGLUT/EAT-4 abundance, whereas those trained to prefer lower temperatures exhibit increased VAChT/UNC-17 abundance. The two transmitters also make distinct, context-dependent contributions to goal-directed navigation. Glutamatergic transmission promotes movement toward the learned thermal preference, whereas cholinergic transmission restrains continued migration beyond it. Analysis of locomotor trajectories further reveals that the two transmitters differentially regulate reorientation decisions across regions of the thermal gradient. Together, these findings identify adaptive co-transmission, a form of synaptic plasticity in which coexisting neurotransmitter systems are differentially organized and regulated by experience, and make distinct, context-dependent contributions to behavior.
articles.author: Cuentas-Condori, A. A., Kumar, S., Agoba, P., Chanaba-Lopez, P., Diaz Garcia, M., Colon-Ramos, D.

articles.title: Hyperglycaemia reversibly disrupts circadian behaviour in mice
articles.content: Disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms are among the most common features of diabetes, and are known to raise the risk of developing the disease. Whether the relationship also runs the other way, with diabetes itself disrupting the clock, has remained unresolved. Using an inducible mouse model of diabetes, in which hyperglycaemia can be induced and then reversed within the same animal, we show that elevated blood glucose is a reversible cause of circadian disruption. Raising blood glucose reduced the amplitude of circadian rest-activity rhythms by 50%, in proportion to the degree of hyperglycaemia, and shortened the free-running period of the clock. Restoring normoglycaemia reversed both effects. Diabetic animals had a delayed phase of activity onset, i.e. later chronotype, and re-entrained more slowly after a simulated jet lag. However, phase shifting to nocturnal light pulses was intact, suggesting normal photic responses. Brain glucose and O-GlcNAcylation, a nutrient-sensitive protein modification, were both elevated in diabetic animals, showing that peripheral hyperglycaemia reaches the brain and alters its metabolic state, and providing a molecular readout of that exposure. Together, these findings establish that a peripheral metabolic state is a reversible determinant of circadian rest-activity behaviour, completing a bidirectional link between blood glucose and the clock and arguing that the two must be treated together rather than in isolation.
articles.author: Lloyd, M., Ni, G., Hu, K.-T., Foster, R. G., Ashcroft, F. M., Jagannath, A., Vasudevan, S. R.

articles.title: Sleep-dependent modulation of thalamic brain temperature estimates in humans
articles.content: Mammalian thermal physiology is geared towards dissipating heat during sleep. Brain temperature typically decreases during non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep in all mammalian species measured to date, yet non-invasive confirmation in healthy humans is lacking: the only available human study used invasive recordings in epileptic patients without a wake control condition. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) enables brain temperature mapping non-invasively, using the temperature-sensitive chemical shift of water relative to N-Acetyl-Aspartate as an internal reference. First, we validated that with metabolite cycling (MC), a MRS approach that enables the simultaneous acquisition of metabolite and water information without conventional water suppression, can be used to determine estimates of brain temperature in an ex vivo sheep head. Next, we determined that by using a temporal resolution of ~4 minutes, we obtained high-quality spectra without losing excessive temporal resolution. We then re-analyzed an existing set of MRS data (acquired with the MC sequence) of the thalamus in young adults (n=9) who slept in the evening for up to 2 hours in the scanner, to assess sleep-evoked changes in estimates of brain temperature. Of the nine participants, five participants took part in the subsequent wake-only experiment, allowing to control for the potential impact of circadian time and body posture on estimates of brain temperature. Sleep-wake states were quantified with standard polysomnography, confirming that the participants managed to sleep in the scanner. On average, they spent 39.4+/-15.7 min in N2 sleep, 24.8+/-18.1 min in N3 sleep, 10.0+/-4.9 min in N1 sleep, and 37.0+/-19.6 min awake. Estimates of brain temperature were correlated across the sleep and wake-only experiment within the same participant (R^2=0.29, P<0.0001). When participants entered NREM sleep, estimates of brain temperature decreased by 0.2 degrees Celcius. Moreover, the deeper NREM sleep, the more pronounced the decrease in estimates of brain temperature (P=0.014). These data suggest that an evening nap consisting of NREM sleep decreases thalamic temperature. Considering the profound impact temperature can have on brain functioning, these brain temperature changes could be a pathway through which sleep impacts the brain.
